strengths: The paper introduces a novel and sensible combination of model soups with self-supervised inter-training, enabling ingredients to be created from unlabeled data and different SSL losses.

It provides the first demonstration (to my knowledge) that linear mode connectivity can hold across ingredients trained with fundamentally different SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR), which is an interesting and potentially useful scientific finding.
The empirical study is broad: 8 ImageNet test sets, 21 VTAB tasks plus 15 corruptions, two stocks (MAE and Franca), and a test-time adaptation comparison with SAR.
The method has practical appeal because it adds no inference cost and can exploit abundant unlabeled data; the gains on corruptions and ImageNet-A, while modest, are in a relevant direction.
The paper introduces Self-Seasoning for label-free mixing and releases a code snippet for it, and it honestly discusses limitations such as the need for unlabeled target data.
Writing is generally clear in motivation, and figures such as the triangle soup plots communicate the LMC/interpolation idea well.
weaknesses: The headline robustness gains (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C) come from inter-training on the unlabeled corrupted test distribution. Even the 'disjoint' split shares the same corruption distribution as the test set, so the result is closer to transductive target adaptation than standard robustness. The crucial baseline—a continued SSL + supervised soup inter-trained on the same corrupted unlabeled data with equal search budget—is missing, so the specific benefit of Self-Souping over simply using unlabeled target data is not isolated.

There are no error bars, confidence intervals, multiple seeds, or significance tests. Many reported gains are below 1% and rankings are inconsistent across tables (e.g., Self-Soup is not best in Table 1 for several columns; Tables 4 and 5 show mixed results), so several claims are not statistically supported.

Self-Seasoning, one of the paper's novel components, is not empirically competitive. In Table 5 it is best on only 4/21 tasks and often much worse than the best ingredient or supervised seasoning (e.g., Clevr-Count 17.5 vs 34.6; dSpr-Loc-X 4.1 vs 11.6). The claim that it is 'competitive' is not supported, and no ablation of the entropy objective or alternative unsupervised selection baselines is provided.

The LMC-across-SSL-algorithms evidence is thin: only three ingredients, one dataset, one stock, and one training schedule, with no interpolation curves/variance beyond final accuracies. The generality of the finding is therefore unclear.

Training is short and may not reflect realistic SSL/transfer regimes: ImageNet inter-training is only 5 epochs, VTAB inter-training is 10K steps, and fine-tuning is 10 epochs. Hyperparameters were 'mostly chosen arbitrarily' and no compute budget, seed, or full tuning protocol is reported.

Reproducibility is incomplete: Appendix C ('Data and Code') is empty in the provided manuscript, there is no repository link, and several dataset references in the appendix are missing from the main bibliography. Training details in Appendix B are too sparse for reliable reproduction.

Missing baselines beyond the continued SSL + supervised soup: the paper does not compare to unsupervised domain adaptation or test-time training methods (except SAR in one small table), to multi-task SSL, or to simple fine-tuning on unlabeled target data without souping. This makes the contribution hard to situate.
The VTAB robustness study uses 1K-sample mini-VTAB and mini-VTAB-C subsets; results may be noisy and are not directly comparable to standard VTAB evaluations.

Presentation quality is uneven: pervasive typo 'Self-Soupervision', 'Self-Soupression' in a figure caption, grammatical errors, and a garbled/strange table in the provided PDF reduce clarity. Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence (e.g., 'countless SSL algorithms', 'competitive' Self-Seasoning).
No theoretical insight or analysis is provided for why LMC holds across different SSL objectives, which limits the paper's scientific depth beyond empirical observation.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely new and well-motivated extension of model soups to self-supervised learning, with a clean formalization (Eq. 2) of inter-training across SSL losses/data prior to supervised fine-tuning.

The finding that linear mode connectivity can hold between ingredients trained with different SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR) is novel and interesting (Fig. 2, Fig. 4), and the exploration over the mixture simplex is a reasonable way to demonstrate it.
Broad empirical sweep: 8 ImageNet test sets plus 21 VTAB tasks evaluated over 15 corruption types, and a bonus comparison against test-time adaptation (SAR).
Proposes Self-Seasoning, an unsupervised way to set mixture coefficients via kNN-entropy minimization, which is a sensible idea for label-free mixing.
The limitations section is candid about the modest gains and the reliance on unlabeled target data.
weaknesses: The headline gains are oversold relative to what the method reliably delivers. The +3.5% (IN-C) and +7% (LAION-C) numbers require inter-training on unlabeled data drawn from the target/shifted distribution, which is a strong and often unavailable assumption, whereas the gains in realistic no-target-data settings are small (e.g., +1% IN-C, +0.4% LAION-C over the continued-SSL baseline in Table 1).

The 'joint' setting in Table 2 uses the same even-indexed test samples for both inter-training and evaluation, which is effectively transductive training on the test set and inflates the reported robustness; the disjoint setting is the only defensible one, and it is weaker.

In Table 1 the Self-Soup 'Best ingredient' row is identical to the continued-SSL 'Best ingredient' row, indicating that SSL inter-training does not improve individual models—only the soup—so the claimed benefit is narrow and the central narrative ('more and better soups') is only partially supported.

Self-Seasoning (Table 5) is 'most accurate on 4/21 tasks' and is clearly worse than supervised seasoning on several tasks (e.g., Clevr-Count 17.5 vs 34.6, DMLab 26.4 vs 35.7). This undercuts the claim that label-free mixing is 'competitive.'

No variance, seeds, or significance testing are reported. Many reported deltas (e.g., ±0.1–0.4%) are plausibly within run-to-run noise, yet the paper makes strong comparative claims; this materially weakens the evidential support.

Comparison fairness is questionable: methods that inter-train on the test distribution (even-indexed samples) obtain information about the evaluation distribution that the supervised and continued-SSL baselines do not, so the robustness comparisons are not apples-to-apples.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. Code and several key details (e.g., exact inter-training schedules, the full Self-Seasoning procedure) are deferred to a supplement that is referenced but not fully shown, and the 'arbitrarily chosen' SSL hyperparameters (Appendix B) raise questions about robustness of the conclusions.

The pervasive cooking metaphor, while charming, frequently obscures the technical content (e.g., the distinction between 'seasoning' and 'Self-Seasoning', 'inter-training' vs 'continued SSL'), making the method harder to parse than necessary.

strengths: Introduces Self-Soups, a broad and natural generalization of model soups to self-supervised learning, enabling ingredients to differ in SSL algorithms, algorithmic hyperparameters, and unlabeled data sources.

Provides the first empirical demonstration that linear mode connectivity can hold between ingredients that differ in their self-supervised training runs, including across three distinct SSL families (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR).
Extensive evaluation across ImageNet variants, ImageNet-C, LAION-C, VTAB, and a new mini-VTAB-C benchmark, with useful gains on robustness and transfer tasks.
Proposes Self-Seasoning, a fully unsupervised way to mix self-supervised ingredients by minimizing kNN prediction entropy, with a code snippet included in the appendix.
Clear writing and informative figures that convey the soup framework and mixture landscapes well, despite the pun-heavy style.
Honest limitations section acknowledging that the largest gains require unlabeled target data, that many gains are modest, and that only three SSL algorithms are studied.
Appendix provides detailed training hyperparameters, optimizer settings, and augmentation choices, aiding reproducibility.
Positive impact statement and use of public benchmarks raise no apparent ethical concerns.
weaknesses: Missing controlled baseline for the shift-inter-training experiments: in §4.3, Self-Soup on corrupted test data is compared to soups trained on clean ImageNet and to a best single ingredient, but not to a non-Self-Soup baseline that also inter-trains on the same unlabeled shift data and then fine-tunes/soups. Thus the reported +3.5% IN-C and +7% LAION-C gains may largely reflect using target-domain data rather than Self-Souping itself.

Most gains are small and reported without error bars or multiple seeds, making it difficult to assess statistical significance. For example, on ImageNet-Val the Self-Soup uniform mix (79.11) is slightly worse than the supervised soup uniform mix (79.12), and several VTAB gains are within ~1%.

The 'Continued SSL + Supervised Soup' baseline is under-specified and may not use the same number of ingredients or search cost as Self-Soups, despite the claim of equal search/development cost. This makes the fairness of the central comparison unclear.

Self-Seasoning is not competitive in the reported results: Table 5 shows it is worse than supervised seasoning and often worse than a uniform soup on many tasks (e.g., Clevr-Count 17.5 vs. 34.6 seasoning, DMLab 26.4 vs. 35.7, dSpr-Loc-X 4.1 vs. 11.6), yet the text calls it 'competitive'. It is best on only 4/21 tasks.

Experiments are at a relatively small scale: ImageNet fine-tuning for 10 epochs, SSL inter-training for 5 epochs or 100K steps, and mini-VTAB subsets of 1K samples. It is unclear whether the findings hold under standard longer schedules or larger models.

The claim that Self-Soupervision 'unlocks countless SSL algorithms' is not fully supported: only three SSL methods are tested, and generalization within the broader space of SSL algorithms is assumed rather than demonstrated.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: the provided PDF shows empty 'Data.' and 'Code.' entries in Appendix C, and the main text does not include a code or data release link, though hyperparameters are detailed.

Presentation has distracting typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'Self-Soupervision' in the title/abstract, misaligned or mislabeled table columns such as 'Metinopathy' instead of 'Retinopathy'), which occasionally obscure the results.

strengths: Introduces Self-Soupervision, a broad and novel generalization of model soups to self-supervised learning. The framework enables soups made from ingredients that differ in SSL algorithm, SSL hyperparameters, unlabeled data source, and/or supervised fine-tuning, which expands the design space of model soups.

Provides the first evidence that linear mode connectivity can hold across ingredients trained with different SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, LeJEPA) and across a different stock (Franca), which is an interesting and non-trivial empirical finding.

Extensive empirical evaluation across ImageNet test sets, corrupted ImageNet, LAION-C, and 21 VTAB tasks with many corruption types. The shift-robustness results are the most convincing: e.g., inter-training on corrupted test data and fine-tuning back on ImageNet gives +3.5% on ImageNet-C and +7% on LAION-C in the disjoint setting (Table 2).

Self-Seasoning is a novel unsupervised mixing procedure that learns mixture coefficients by minimizing kNN entropy. It is competitive with labeled seasoning in the few-shot regime (Figure 4, Table 9), enabling soups without any labels at the mixing stage.

Practical motivation is clear: soups preserve inference cost, and Self-Soups can exploit unlabeled target/shifted data. The limitations section honestly notes the main caveat that the largest gains require unlabeled shifted data.
The appendix provides substantial hyperparameter details for inter-training, fine-tuning, TTA, and few-shot seasoning, which helps reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is insufficient. There are no error bars, random seeds, or significance tests. Many reported gains are tiny (e.g., Table 1: Self-Soup greedy 79.41 vs supervised 79.34 on IN-Val; Self-Soup 29.90 vs supervised 29.92 on IN-R; Table 4 mean 19.9 vs 19.4 vs 19.3), so the central claims about improvements over baselines are not reliably established.

Confounds between souping, extra compute, and extra unlabeled data are not fully controlled. Self-Soups use additional SSL inter-training runs and M*N total training runs, but the paper does not compare against a single model trained with equal total compute (e.g., longer fine-tuning or a longer continued-SSL run). Comparisons to supervised soups and best ingredients therefore conflate the benefit of souping with the benefit of more training.

The VTAB transfer results are marginal and inconsistent. Table 4 shows small average gains and several tasks where Self-Soups underperform. The claim that Self-Souping transfers well across 21 tasks is not strongly supported by the evidence.

Reproducibility is weakened by incomplete code/data availability: the main text gives only 'https://github.com/' and Appendix D says only 'Data. Code.' without actual links, seeds, or exact splits. This makes it difficult to verify the results or build on the method.

The Self-Seasoning method is not clearly specified mathematically. Equation 3 defines similarities, probabilities, and an entropy objective, but does not explicitly show how the mixture coefficients alpha enter the embedding computation, nor how alpha weights are normalized or optimized in practice. This hinders both understanding and reproducibility.

Presentation is difficult to parse. The food metaphor is pervasive, Table 4 is misaligned/hard to read, and some claims are overstated (e.g., 'unlocks countless SSL algorithms', 'more accurate than any single SSL ingredient', 'first to show' LMC across SSL algorithms). The abstract emphasizes +7% but this requires access to unlabeled shifted data, as the limitations note.

The evidence for LMC across different SSL algorithms is limited to four algorithms, short inter-training (5 epochs on ImageNet), and one dataset setting. It is unclear whether the finding would hold for longer SSL training, larger algorithm families, or more diverse unlabeled distributions.

Some baselines may not be fully fair. In the test-distribution experiments, Self-Soups use corrupted test samples (even-indexed) for inter-training, whereas supervised soups do not have this access. The joint setting uses test samples for both inter-training and evaluation, which is transductive and not comparable to standard robustness evaluation.

strengths: Novel and genuinely interesting core finding: the paper shows linear mode connectivity (LMC) can hold between ingredients produced by *different* SSL algorithms (MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, LeJEPA), extending model soups beyond supervised fine-tuning. This is a new and potentially influential observation that could motivate follow-up work.

Broad and thorough empirical evaluation: seven extra ImageNet test sets, 21 VTAB tasks, a self-built mini-VTAB-C with 15 corruptions (336 test sets), and a second stock (Franca) to show the effect is not MAE-specific.
Self-Seasoning is a genuinely new, fully unsupervised mixture method (entropy minimization over kNN predictions) that is competitive with labeled seasoning on small-sample natural tasks (Fig. 4).

Baselines are reasonable and control for search cost: the 'continued SSL + supervised soup' baseline has equal development cost to Self-Soups, and the comparison against Model Ratatouille (Tab. 5) is well constructed.
The limitations section is honest, explicitly acknowledging that the largest gains require unlabeled target data and that other gains are modest (<1%).
weaknesses: The headline numbers (+3.5% ImageNet-C, +7% LAION-C) come from inter-training on the *unlabeled test distribution* (even-indexed corrupted test samples), i.e., transductive/unsupervised domain adaptation to the target shift. Doing better on a distribution you have (unlabeled) access to is largely expected, and the framing oversells self-supervision as the source of the gain; the paper itself concedes it is related to UDA/TTA.

Controlled gains are marginal: in Tab. 1/Tab. 7, the Self-Soup uniform mix beats the continued-SSL baseline by only ~0.6-0.9% on corrupted sets and is essentially tied on IN-Val/IN-ReaL/IN-V2; on VTAB (Tab. 4) the margin is ~0.5%. On structured VTAB tasks and noise corruptions, Self-Soups actually underperform the baselines.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are reported, despite differences of well under 1%. The VTAB/seasoning results additionally select the 'best of 6' hyperparameter settings, which introduces selection bias and further weakens the marginal comparisons.

Reproducibility is materially compromised: the code link is literally truncated ('https://github.com/'), and the appendix 'Data.' and 'Code.' sections are empty placeholders; mini-VTAB-C is only 'shared in the supplement,' which is not present. This makes it hard for others to build on the contribution.

The §4.1 experiment that establishes the central LMC claim uses very short SSL inter-training (5 epochs at 1e-5 LR) before 10-epoch fine-tuning, so the ingredients may be barely distinct from the shared stock; the claim that soups work across SSL algorithms would be much stronger with evidence that the ingredients are genuinely diverse (e.g., representation/weight distance, longer inter-training).

The mechanism is not analyzed: the paper asserts 'LMC can thus hold' but offers no explanation for *why* ingredients from different SSL losses remain linearly connected after fine-tuning, and the 'first to show' claims are somewhat overstated given soups already work across hyperparameters and datasets.

Presentation is weakened by the heavy cooking metaphor ('stock', 'ingredients', 'soup', 'seasoning', 'flavor'), numerous typos, and citation inconsistencies (e.g., LeJEPA cited as 2023 in text but 2025 in references), which reduce clarity.

strengths: Novel and interesting empirical finding: the paper is the first to show that linear mode connectivity (LMC) can hold between ingredients that differ in their self-supervised training runs—even across fundamentally different SSL algorithm families (pixel-reconstruction MAE, instance-contrastive MoCoV3, dimension-contrastive MMCR/LeJEPA). This is a genuinely new contribution to the soups/merging literature.

Generalizes model soups to unlabeled data, which expands the space of usable data sources (transfer data, shifted/target distributions) and losses, and the framework is cleanly formalized in Eq. 2 as an extension of the Model Ratatouille formulation with labels removed from the inter-training stage.

Self-Seasoning is a clean, fully unsupervised mixing method (kNN-entropy minimization over mixture coefficients) that is shown to be competitive with labeled seasoning and to beat fine-tuning in the low-label regime (<500 samples), which is a useful practical result.

Evaluation breadth is good: eight ImageNet test sets, VTAB with 21 tasks x 16 clean/corrupt conditions (336 test sets), an additional stock (Franca), and a second augmentation scheme (RandAug) in the appendix.

Honest and well-scoped limitations discussion: the authors explicitly note that the largest gains need unlabeled target/shifted data, that other gains are modest, and that only a few SSL families are studied.
Reasonable reproducibility: code link provided, plus detailed training hyperparameters, optimizer/schedule settings, and even PyTorch code for the Self-Seasoning objective in the appendix.
The comparison against Model Ratatouille (Tab. 5) is a fair and informative control, showing that Self-Souping matches a supervised inter-training recipe without needing auxiliary labeled datasets.
weaknesses: The reported gains are small in most settings. In Tab. 1/7 the Self-Soup advantage over the continued-SSL + supervised soup on IN-C/LAION-C is only ~0.5-0.9%, and on VTAB the mean advantage is ~0.5% (19.9 vs 19.4/19.3). Several of these differences are plausibly within run-to-run noise, and no variance or significance testing is reported anywhere.

The headline results (+3.5% IN-C, +7% LAION-C) depend on inter-training on samples drawn from the test distribution (even-indexed test samples). While the even/odd split is a defensible protocol, this is essentially transductive use of target data, and the paper's framing ('shift-aware ingredients') sometimes underplays how much the gain relies on target-distribution availability rather than the souping mechanism itself.

Results on VTAB are mixed: the Self-Soup loses to the supervised-only soup on several specialized/structured tasks, and the paper's own table (Tab. 4b) shows it is worse on noise corruptions. The 'natural data' advantage is real but narrow.

The paper never explains *why* LMC should hold across ingredients trained with different SSL objectives. The central claim is purely empirical; even a heuristic argument (e.g., relating to shared stock basin / low-loss path) would substantially strengthen the contribution.

The cooking metaphor is pervasive (stock, ingredients, soup, seasoning, flavor, 'tasty') and, while charming, comes at a real cost to technical clarity. Key methodological distinctions (e.g., precisely what constitutes a Self-Soup vs. a continued-SSL soup, and the exact search-cost accounting) are harder to parse than necessary.

The 'best ingredient' and 'greedy search' rows are selected on IN-Val accuracy, which the authors acknowledge means greedy may not rank first on the target metric. This makes several baseline numbers (e.g., best-ingredient values in Tab. 2) confusing and complicates fair comparison across rows.

Self-Seasoning (§4.6) is evaluated on 1K-sample mini-VTAB subsets with kNN classification, a fairly small-scale and noisy setting; the claim that it is 'competitive with labeled seasoning' rests on small absolute differences across many tasks.

The claim that Self-Soupervision 'unlocks countless SSL algorithms' is speculative; the study covers three families plus one fresh method, and the authors themselves note the need to check generalization within families.
